- `go.sh` prints this line first. 4864 is the process id of the shell that runs `go.sh` [Ref1].
- The text in brackets is a hint for the operator. The command `kill -TERM -- -4864` sends the signal TERM (a request to stop) to every process of the process group 4864 [Ref13].
- The hint works only when `go.sh` is the first process of its own process group. This was the case. The start command ran `go.sh` through the tool `setsid`, which starts a program in a new process group [Ref15].
segments.heading: Start of the log

segments.text:
- `go.sh` prints the Linux kernel command line from the file `/proc/cmdline` [Ref1]. The next bullets explain the options that matter for the test.
- `BOOT_IMAGE=`: the file of the Linux kernel that was started. Its release name is `7.1.3-arm-agi-20260916-v0.7.2-g4dbc8bb88858` [Ref4].
- `isolcpus=domain,managed_irq,126-127`: a boot setting that isolates CPUs 126 and 127 from the scheduler [Ref6] [Ref7]. The test uses CPUs 0 to 119 only.
- `irqaffinity=0-119`: the default CPUs for the handling of interrupts are CPUs 0 to 119 [Ref8]. These are the CPUs of the test.
- `cpufreq.default_governor=performance`: the governor that each CPU gets at boot [Ref8]. Line 3 shows the governors at the time of the run.
- `rcupdate.rcu_normal=1`: the Linux kernel uses only the normal form of one of its internal waits (the RCU grace period), not the expedited (faster) form [Ref8]. Notes of 2026-10-30 about the tests of another user on CRB say that this option and the three options before it were added to the command line on 2026-10-22 [Ref7]. The same notes say that a latency test of that user pins its threads to CPUs 120 to 127 [Ref7].
segments.heading: Machine settings, read once before the first step (lines 2 to 5)

segments.text:
`go.sh` reads the governor of each CPU from 0 to 119 (file `cpufreq/scaling_governor` of the CPU) and counts equal names [Ref1].
- ` 120 performance;`: all 120 CPUs have the governor `performance`. This governor requests the highest frequency inside the limits that are set for the CPU [Ref9].
- `cpu0 scaling_cur_freq 2800000`: the frequency that Linux reports for CPU 0. The unit is kHz, so the value is 2.8 GHz [Ref9]. By the Linux documentation it is in most cases the frequency that Linux last requested from the hardware. It can differ from the frequency at which the CPU runs [Ref9].
- Only CPU 0 is read for the frequency. The log holds no frequency of the 119 other CPUs.

`go.sh` prints the two settings of Linux for transparent huge pages (2 MiB pages) [Ref1]. The word in square brackets is the active value [Ref4].
- `enabled` is `always`: Linux may place any anonymous memory of a program on 2 MiB pages. Anonymous memory is memory without a file behind it, for example from `malloc`. The program does not have to ask [Ref10].
- `defrag` is `madvise`: when no 2 MiB block is free, a page fault waits for Linux to make one only in memory that the program marked with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` [Ref10].
- These are settings. Whether a benchmark buffer lay on 2 MiB pages is not in this file. The `P` rows of the bwx12 csv files record it for parts L and C. For part A it is not recorded [Ref4].

`taskset -cp` prints the CPU list of the shell that runs `go.sh` (process 4864): CPUs 0 to 119 [Ref1].
- A process that this shell starts gets the same list [Ref13]. So `ra.sh`, `rx.sh` and their helper commands run on CPUs 0 to 119. These are also the CPUs of the benchmark threads.
- The scripts set this list again for the benchmark processes. `ra.sh` restarts itself through `taskset -c 0-119` (a tool that starts a program with the given CPU list). `rx.sh` starts bwx12 the same way [Ref2] [Ref3].
- `go.sh` holds no command that sets its own list. The start command holds none either [Ref15]. So the shell got the list from the process that started it.
- An inspection of CRB on 2026-10-30 found the setting `CPUAffinity=0-119` of systemd (the program that runs as the first process of the system). It gives this list to that process and to every process that descends from it [Ref6]. The scripts of the rerun do not read this setting.

State before the first step, printed by the function `state` of `go.sh` [Ref1]. Fields from left to right:
- `== start`: the label that the caller passes. `utc`: the time on the clock of CRB in UTC, from the command `date -u`.
- `boot`: the boot id, read from the file `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`. Before the first step `go.sh` tests that it is the id of the boot in which 12 memory modules at 7200 MT/s were recorded.
- `MemTotal:`: the line `MemTotal` of the file `/proc/meminfo`. It is the usable memory that Linux reports, here 395392808 kB. Before the first step `go.sh` requires at least 395000000 kB as the sign of 12 modules.
- `load`: the content of the file `/proc/loadavg`, five fields. The row of line 8 explains them. Here the 1-minute load average is 0.07.
- `users 0`: the number of lines that the tool `who` prints, one line per login. `marker absent`: the marker file does not exist.
- `processes per user:`: the tool `ps` prints the user name of every process of the machine, and the script counts equal names. The log holds these counts only. It does not name the processes.

State after step T72A1. `go.sh` prints it when `ra.sh` has returned: 22:13:29, 80 s after the line `start`. It is also the state before step T72L1. The five fields of `load` [Ref5]:
- `80.50 24.65 8.59`: the load average over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A load average is the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux.
- `1/1018`: 1 task is runnable at this moment, and 1018 tasks exist.
- `8014`: the process id of the newest process on the machine.
- The 1-minute value was 0.07 in line 6. Between the two lines part A ran 24 processes with 120 threads each.

Output of the last line of `rx.sh` for step T72L1 (part L of session 1, one bwx12 process) [Ref3].
- `done`: the result folder. It holds `a6456.csv` (the rows that bwx12 printed), `env.txt`, `launches.txt` and `stderr.txt`. `rx.sh` started at 22:13:29.
- `2`: the number of non-empty lines in `launches.txt`. They are one `launch` line and one `rc` line of the one process.
- `0`: the number of bytes in `stderr.txt`. So bwx12 wrote nothing to its error output.
- Between the two numbers `rx.sh` would print each `rc` line with an exit status other than 0. After the second number it would print the first 600 bytes of `stderr.txt`. Neither is present.

segments.heading: End of the run

segments.text:
Last line that `go.sh` prints. The script reaches it only when it did not stop before. It stops with a line `FAILED:` in three cases [Ref1]:
- a check at its start fails
- `ra.sh` or `rx.sh` returns a status other than 0
- `rxok` does not find exactly one `rc` line with status 0
After the line `FAILED:` the script prints one state line with the label `abort` and ends with status 1. The analysis scripts test for the line `ALLDONE` and for lines that start with `FAILED` [Ref11] [Ref12].
